chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
title: Day jobs: cooking and bartending
summary: Rosenberg talks about his own short-order cook and bartending jobs.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: I did some sheet rock once. Usually when I was working day jobs I'd work some -- I did some cooking jobs, you know, short order cook, stuff like that.
Can you cook?
Yeah.
You can cook, too?
Yeah. I used to, you know, And bartend sometimes. Bartending is a joke, as far as I'm concerned.
Yeah.
There's nothing to it. Everyone makes a big deal about it, you know.
Yeah. The only thing you've got to do is watch that glass breaking in the place, you know.
Yeah. But they have a micocologist's school and all this kind of nonsense, you know.
Yeah.
I learned to bartend in about a week and a half, and I could do everything, you know. Like these weird off the wall drinks, you know.
Yeah. Did you like it?
Well, I was working mostly service bar, you know, which is like you don't have to deal directly with the customer.
Yeah, right.
If you have to deal with the customers and all that kind of stuff, that can get to be a chore, because everybody thinks you're their mother or something, you know.
Yeah, it's a hassle.
It's a hassle. But what I was doing was I was just working in a restaurant, you know.
Uh-huh.
A service bar.
Yeah.
You know, you split the tips with the waiter.
Yeah.
And, you know, it's usually good tips.
Uh-huh.
So, you know, it wasn't bad.
Well, that was a good gig.
